# Files and formats

Ask NCBI for `NM_007294.4` and it'll hand you that record as FASTA, or as a
GenBank flatfile, and those two files share almost nothing except the letters.
Pull the raw reads behind it out of a public archive and you get a third
format. Ask which bases differ between one person's genome and the reference
and you get a fourth. All of them are current. The oldest was designed in 1985
and nobody is retiring it. So why does one field need this many ways to write
down a sequence, and why does the count only ever go up?

## A format is a decision about what to leave out

The FASTA version of `NM_007294.4` is a header line and 7,088 bases, and that's
the entire file. It won't tell you which organism the sequence came from, and
it won't tell you that the coding part starts at base 114.

The GenBank version of the same record carries all of that, plus the papers
NCBI has attached to the record. It's the same 7,088 bases with several hundred
lines bolted on top.

Neither file is better. They answer different questions. FASTA is small and
every program on earth reads it. GenBank is large and takes real work to parse,
and it's the only one of the two that can tell you where an exon ends.

One rule comes out of that, and it'll save you an afternoon. Going
down is easy: any tool can throw the annotation away and write you a FASTA.
Going up is impossible. Once a file has been cut back to a name and some
letters, nothing gets the coordinates back, and you'll be fetching the record
all over again.

## FASTA holds the least of any of them

You met FASTA in Chapter 5. Here's the part that chapter didn't need yet.

``` {.default filename="data/sequences/messy.fasta"}
>NM_007294.4 Homo sapiens BRCA1 mRNA, wrapped
GCTGAGACTTCCTGGACGGGGGACAGGCTGTGGGGTTTCTCAGATAACTGGGCCCCTGCG
CTCAGGAGGCCTTCACCCTCTGCTCTGGGTAAAGTTCATTGGAACAGAAAGAAATGGATT
TATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCATTAATGCTATGCAGAAAATCTTAG
```

Those line breaks carry no meaning. I wrapped that record at sixty characters
because the script that built the file was set to sixty. Other files come at
seventy, at eighty, or with no break at all, and nothing in a FASTA file
records which. A parser has to glue the lines back together before it counts
anything. The next record in that same file puts all 420 of its bases on one
unbroken line, which is too wide to print here. Both records are legal.

So the length of a FASTA record isn't a property you can see. You have to
compute it, and the file will not help you.

Chapter 5 warned you about the rest of the header. Most software keeps
everything up to the first space and drops the remainder, so the header above
goes in as `NM_007294.4`. Now look at the fourth record in that file. Its header
starts `>NM_007294.4_translated`, and one underscore is all that keeps it out of
the first record's slot. Put a space there instead and the fourth record lands
on top of the first, and four records quietly become three. Exercise 15.1 asks
what a parser should do about it.

FASTA is everywhere. Sequence goes into a website in FASTA and comes out of a
website in FASTA, and it has done that since 1985, when David J. Lipman and
William R. Pearson published the search program the format was invented for.

## FASTQ adds how much to trust each letter

Raw output from a sequencing machine arrives as [FASTQ]{.term def="A four-line-per-read text format: a name line starting with an at sign, the bases, a plus line, then one quality character per base."},
which is FASTA with a confidence attached to every base. Four lines make one
read. I typed the two below by hand for this page. The bases are real: read 1
is bases 1 to 40 of `NM_007294.4`, and read 2 is bases 61 to 100.

``` {.default}
@demo_read_1
GCTGAGACTTCCTGGACGGGGGACAGGCTGTGGGGTTTCT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII?????55,
@demo_read_2
CTCAGGAGGCCTTCACCCTCTGCTCTGGGTAAAGTTCATT
+
@IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII??????5,
```

Line one is the read name and starts with `@`. Line two is the bases. Line
three is a `+` and usually holds nothing else. Line four is the quality string,
one character per base, in the same order as line two.

Each quality character stands for a number. Take its position in the ASCII
table and subtract 33. `I` is ASCII 73, so `I` means 40. `?` is 63, so `?`
means 30. `5` is 53, so `5` means 20. That number is a [Phred quality score]{.term def="A number saying how likely a base call is wrong. Q20 is one error in a hundred, Q30 is one in a thousand."},
and each 10 points is a factor of ten in the error rate. A `5` says the machine
puts the odds of that letter being wrong at one in a hundred. A `?` says one in
a thousand. The run of `I` at the front of both reads says one in ten thousand.
Each read ends on a comma, which is ASCII 44 and means 11, a shade better than
one error in ten.

::: {.why}
A sequencing machine never reads a base. It reads a measurement and guesses a
letter from it, and some guesses are far shakier than others. The quality
string is the machine telling you which ones. Reads usually get worse toward
their far end, which is why the two above decay from `I` down through `5` to a
comma.
:::

Count the characters on line two and line four of either read. Both are 40.
They always match, and that's the one check you can run on a FASTQ file without
any tool at all.

::: {.trap}
`@` is a legal quality character. It's ASCII 64, so it means 31, and a quality
line is allowed to start with one. Count the lines in that block that start with
`@`. Three do, and there are two reads, because the quality line of
`demo_read_2` starts with one. Count reads that way and your number comes out
too big, with nothing to tell you so. Count lines and divide by four instead.
:::

You'll meet FASTQ the moment you pull raw data off a public archive. Work out
what it costs first. The sequence costs one character per base, and the quality
line costs one more. That puts the same letters at over twice the size of a
FASTA. An archive also holds every read an experiment produced rather than one
finished sequence. This book never asks you to download one.

## GenBank holds everything, coordinates included

The [GenBank flatfile]{.term def="NCBI's full text record for one sequence: description, references, annotated features with coordinates, then the sequence itself."}
is what you get when nothing is left out. Ask NCBI for `NM_007294.4` and take
the GenBank view of the record rather than the FASTA one, and this is the real
text that comes back.

``` {.default}
LOCUS       NM_007294               7088 bp    mRNA    linear   PRI 04-JUN-2026
...
FEATURES             Location/Qualifiers
     source          1..7088
                     /organism="Homo sapiens"
                     /mol_type="mRNA"
                     ...
     exon            1..94
                     /gene="BRCA1"
                     ...
     exon            95..193
                     /gene="BRCA1"
                     ...
     CDS             114..5705
                     /gene="BRCA1"
                     ...
```

Each `...` is a cut I made to fit the page. The real record runs past six
hundred lines before the sequence itself starts.

Read the left column as a list of features and the right column as where each
one sits. `1..7088` is the whole transcript. `114..5705` is the coding range
you subtracted in Chapter 5, and now you can see the file it came out of.

The two dots mean "through, and include both ends". So `1..94` is 94 bases:
94 minus 1, plus 1. The next exon starts at 95, because 94 was used up.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI interface on 2 August 2026. The control that
switches a record between its FASTA view and its GenBank view has moved and
been renamed more than once. What stays true is that one accession has both
views, and the letters are identical in each.
:::

Reach for a flatfile on any NCBI record where you need the annotation and not
only the letters.

## BED is three columns and a counting convention

A [BED]{.term def="A tab-separated interval format. Sequence name, start, end. Coordinates count from zero and the end position is not included."}
file says nothing about sequence. It's a list of intervals, tab separated, with
three required columns: what you're on, where the interval starts, where it
ends. Here are the same two exons, written by hand as BED.

``` {.default}
NM_007294.4	0	94	exon1	0	+
NM_007294.4	94	193	exon2	0	+
```

The first column doesn't have to be a chromosome. BED wants a sequence name and
two numbers, and it has no opinion about what the sequence is. The three fields
after them are optional: a label, a score this file has no use for, and the
strand.

Then the part that matters: BED counts from zero, and the end position is not
part of the interval. So the first exon runs `0 94`, and the second one starts
at `94`, the same number that ended the first. They don't overlap. Chapter 11
taught you that shape already: `seq[0:94]` and `seq[94:193]` in Python are
those two exons exactly.

BED turns up in genome browsers, and in any tool that asks you which regions
you care about.

## VCF stores differences, not sequence

[VCF]{.term def="Variant Call Format. One line per position where a sample differs from a named reference, with the reference and the alternate bases."}
holds the positions where a sample disagrees with a reference genome, and
nothing else. Storing a whole genome per person would be enormous and almost
entirely repetition, so the format stores the disagreements. Here's a small one
I wrote by hand.

``` {.default}
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=<ID=demo,length=300>
#CHROM	POS	ID	REF	ALT	QUAL	FILTER	INFO
demo	120	.	C	T	.	PASS	DP=44
demo	147	.	AGG	A	.	PASS	DP=39
```

Lines beginning with `##` are the header, and they're where the format records
which reference the file was called against. A single line starts with one `#`
and names the columns. Everything after that is one variant per line.

The first variant says position 120 is `C` in the reference and `T` in this
sample. The second one is a deletion, and it looks stranger than it is. `AGG`
against `A` means the `GG` at 148 and 149 is gone. VCF carries the base in
front of a deletion so that the line still has something to point at, which is
why the position reads 147 rather than 148.

`POS` counts from one. A dot means "no value here", not zero.

Those eight columns are the ones every VCF has. A file with genotypes in it
adds a `FORMAT` column after `INFO` and then one column per sample, so a study
of twelve people carries twelve more columns on the right.

::: {.trap}
A VCF is meaningless without the reference it was called against, and the
reference is named in a header line that most viewers hide. Chapter 5's two
coordinates for the same variant, 41,276,045 and 43,124,028, are the same
hazard. Load a GRCh37 file into a GRCh38 browser and every variant lands
somewhere plausible and wrong.
:::

Every paper that reports variants stands on a VCF, and so does every clinical
genetics pipeline in existence.

## The same exon, two coordinate systems

Chapter 11 gave you the rule for crossing between Python's counting and a
database's: the start moves, the stop doesn't. Here's why that rule outlives
Python. The two counting systems aren't a quirk of one language. They're built
into the file formats themselves, and most of the conversions you'll ever do
are between two files.

Two conventions are in use, both of them everywhere.

| Format | First base is | End position |
|---|---|---|
| BED | 0 | not included |
| GFF and GTF | 1 | included |
| VCF | 1 | included |
| GenBank features | 1 | included |

Take the first exon of `NM_007294.4`. GenBank writes it `1..94`. BED writes it
`0 94`. Both describe the identical 94 bases, and you can check that from the
two lengths:

``` {.default}
GenBank:  94 - 1 + 1  =  94 bases
BED:      94 - 0      =  94 bases
```

GFF writes the same exon across nine tab-separated columns, with the start and
the end sitting in the fourth and the fifth.

``` {.default}
NM_007294.4	.	exon	1	94	.	+	.	ID=exon1
```

A dot in a GFF column means the file has no value to put there. Everything else
in that row agrees with the BED row above it, except the one number this whole
section is about.

A feature that's 94 bases long is 94 bases long in every one of these formats.
The start number differs by one. The end number comes out the same, because
BED's end sits one past the last base and GFF's end sits on it. That's the
whole conversion: subtract one from the start, and leave the end alone.

::: {.check}
Do the second exon before reading on. GenBank says `95..193`. Write the BED
row. You should get `94 193`, and both formats should give you 99 bases:
193 minus 95 plus 1, and 193 minus 94. If you wrote `95 193` you converted the
start twice, which is the error this section exists to prevent.
:::

The conversion is one subtraction. Knowing that you need to do it is the part
that costs people a day.

<!-- nlr-allow: 43124027 -->

::: {.trap}
A file never says which convention it uses, and no tool checks. A BED row
copied straight into a GFF column shifts the feature one base to the left and
makes it one base longer. Do that to a coding region and the codon boundaries
move, so Chapter 13's translator hands you a different protein and no error.
It goes wrong in the other direction too. Browser search boxes take 1-based
coordinates, so a BED start of 43,124,027 typed into one lands you on the base
before the one you meant.
:::

## Walkthrough: opening a file in Colab

A running program is always standing in some folder, and a path is directions
from there. In Colab you start in a folder called `/content`. A path with no
slash in front of it gets read from wherever you're standing, so `messy.fasta`
means the file next to you and `data/sequences/messy.fasta` means two folders
down.

Open a file, read all of it into a string, and look at the shape of what you
got.

```{python}
text = open("data/sequences/messy.fasta").read()
lines = text.splitlines()

n = 0
for line in lines:
    if line.startswith(">"):
        n = n + 1

print(len(text), "characters")
print(len(lines), "lines")
print(n, "records")
```

<!-- nlr-allow: 1790 -->

That output came from running the cell with the file sitting in
`data/sequences/`. If your copy of `messy.fasta` sits next to the notebook
instead, change the path to `"messy.fasta"` and nothing else in the cell
changes.

`.read()` gives you the file as one long string. `.splitlines()` cuts it at the
line breaks and hands back a list, which is the form you want almost every
time. Four records in 25 lines, and you already know those four aren't the same
shape as each other.

### Writing a file, and the flag that empties it

You read a file with one argument. You write one with two, and the second
argument is the part to be careful with.

``` {.python}
with open("ids.txt", "w") as out:
    out.write("NM_007294.4\n")
    out.write("NM_009764.3\n")

print(open("ids.txt").read())
```

``` {.default .output}
NM_007294.4
NM_009764.3

```

That `"w"` means write. The `with` block closes the file for you when it ends,
and a file that never gets closed can arrive on disk half-written. `\n` is a
line break, and `.write()` won't add one for you, so two writes with no `\n`
land on the same line.

::: {.trap}
`"w"` empties the file before it writes anything. Point it at a file you spent
an evening building and that file is now zero bytes, with no warning, no
confirmation and no undo. The flag that adds to the end instead is `"a"`. Read
the second argument every time you type it.
:::

### Keeping your work: mounting Drive

Colab lends you a runtime, and the runtime goes away with everything you wrote
on it. Run these two lines and your Google Drive shows up as a folder inside
that runtime.

``` {.python}
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount("/content/drive")
```

``` {.default .output}
Mounted at /content/drive
```

Your files are then under `/content/drive/MyDrive`, and a path that starts
there survives the runtime being recycled. You'll be asked to approve the
connection first, and the approval is per session.

::: {.asof}
Checked against Colab on 2 August 2026. The approval step has changed shape
more than once. What stays true is that mounting needs your permission, the
mount point is a folder you pick, and your own files land under `MyDrive`.
:::

## Why none of these will ever go away

GenBank release 3 came out in December 1982 with 606 entries and 680,338 bases
in it. Release 272 was current when I checked in August 2026, and it counts
192,425,204 entries and 79,604,775,262 bases the same way. That's the
like-for-like column of NCBI's own growth table, and the whole of GenBank is
far bigger again once whole-genome shotgun data is counted. The flatfile you
read three pages ago is that same format. It has been extended since, and it
has never been replaced.

That's the answer to the opening question. Every format here was designed by
somebody solving a problem they had that week, and it stuck because other
people's files were in it. Deprecate a format now and you break the published
record, so nobody does it. Formats accumulate. They don't get replaced.

Here's what to do about it. Don't wait for the field to settle on one
file type, and don't learn a format by reading its specification. Open the file
and look at the first few lines, because five minutes of looking answers more
questions than an hour of reading about it.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="15.1" time="45 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Write a parser for `data/sequences/messy.fasta` that uses no library at all,
and print what's in the file.
:::
::: {.given}
Four records. Every defect in the file is one that somebody has really sent
somebody else. The first record is wrapped at 60 columns and the second has its
whole sequence on one line. A blank line sits inside the third. Every header
has spaces in it. The last record ends in a `*`, left behind by a tool that
marks the stop codon. None of this is invalid FASTA, and all of it breaks a
parser written in a hurry.
:::
::: {.produce}
One line per record, in the order the records appear in the file: the
identifier, then the length of the sequence in bases. Take the identifier to be
everything after the `>` up to the first space, and don't count the `*` as a
base.
:::
::: {.check}
Four lines, and the lengths are 480, 420, 480 and 180. If your third record
comes out at 240 you stopped reading at the blank line. If your last one is 181
you counted the `*`. If three of your four lengths come out at 60 or 61 you're
keeping the last line of each record instead of joining them. Record 2 looks
right only because its whole sequence is one line. If you got fewer than four
lines your loop is overwriting a record. Last part: `NM_007294.4` and
`NM_007294.4_translated` are two identifiers separated by one underscore. Say
what your parser should do if that underscore were a space.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="2.4in"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'messy.fasta'"}
Python is talking, and it's telling you where it looked. It searched the folder
the notebook is standing in, which is `/content` unless you moved. Either the
file isn't there or the name is off by a character. Print the folder's contents
before you retype the path.
:::

::: {.errfix err="UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x8b in position 1: invalid start byte"}
The file is compressed and you opened it as text. A name ending in `.gz` is the
tell, and `0x8b` is the second byte every gzip file starts with. Python did
exactly what you asked. Uncompress the file first, or open it with a reader
that handles gzip.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: I/O operation on closed file."}
You used a file after its `with` block ended. The block closes the handle on
the way out, on purpose. Move the code that reads the file inside the block, or
read everything into a variable while the block is still open.
:::

::: {.errfix err="TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int"}
`.write()` takes text only. A number has to be converted first: `str(480)`
rather than `480`. Nothing about the file is wrong.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name what each of FASTA, FASTQ, GenBank, BED and VCF holds, and one place
  you'd meet each one
- Check a FASTQ record by comparing the length of its sequence line and its
  quality line
- Convert one quality character into a Phred score, and say what that score
  claims about the base
- Convert a GenBank feature range into a BED row, and confirm both give the
  same length
- Read a file into a string in Colab, write a file back out, and say what `"w"`
  does to a file that already exists
- Explain why a VCF is unusable without the name of its reference
:::
